chapter_theme: Neelakesi presses Mokkalan on eating flesh, answering his defence by intention with the seller who kills for the buyer's price and the teacher whose permission sustains the killing; worsted, he attacks Jain bodily mortification as profitless self-torment, and she answers with the Buddha's own ten perfections and ascetic rules and the bodhisattva's praised sufferings, then attacks the gift of the body as a killing of the lives within it, and begins to defend the Jain view that plants have life.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Buddhist elder at Padumapuram, named in 266 as the Buddha's first disciple and Arkkachandra's teacher

342.reading: Neelakesi argues that the noble, who shun toddy as they shun poison, ought by the same reasoning to shun flesh, and asks where an ascetic firm in truth is to be found when the one who takes flesh and eats it is none other than Mokkalan.
342.nuance: The argument works from a ban the Buddhists already keep: the monk renounces toddy, so the debater asks why the same judgement stops short of meat. The last line turns the general question into a charge against the elder himself.

claims.claim: one who shuns intoxicating liquor as harmful must for the same reason shun flesh

343.reading: She says that if the brahmins' scripture and his own are both claimed to bring benefit, she can grant what each tells one to give up and to take, but since both speak only of things that are not clean, he has never had a sharp judgement.
343.nuance: The verse pairs the Buddhist scripture with the brahmins' (பார்ப்பனி ஓத்து) as alike in allowing what is unclean, which in context means flesh. The middle lines are hard to construe and the reading given is tentative.

344.reading: She grants, for argument, his plea that the eater incurs no evil deed because he never thought of consuming the small creatures in the flesh, and answers that the sellers of meat want only the price, not the deed, so the killing is done for the buyer.
344.nuance: This answers the Buddhist defence by intention: the eater did not will the death. The reply moves the question from the eater's mind to the market, where the merchant's motive is the price the eater pays. Line 3 (ஓவெனு முன்) is obscure.

claims.claim: one who eats flesh without intending harm to any creature incurs no evil deed
the seller kills for the buyer's price, so the eater's lack of intent does not free him from the killing

345.reading: She recalls his saying that those who join in acts such as pulling out an arrow already lodged in a beast are not touched by the deed, and asks who here shows compassion by eating while pleading such excuses.
345.nuance: The example of the lodged arrow seems to stand for every share in a death that comes after the blow; the debater treats it as a loophole. Line 3 and the word கடம் in line 4 are unclear, so the sense of the comparison is uncertain.

claims.claim: those who only take part after the killing, as by drawing out the arrow, are not bound by its deed

346.reading: She turns his own teaching back on him: if, as he says, a demon with a mind set on eating earns a lasting evil deed, then by his own words the will to eat is what binds, and the one who eats is bound.
346.nuance: The Buddhist emphasis on intention, used in 344 to excuse the eater, is here made to condemn him: the desire to eat is an intention too. The figure of the demon (பேய்) may glance at Neelakesi's own past as a flesh-taking demoness. Lines 2 and 3 do not construe clearly.

claims.claim: a mind set on eating flesh is itself enough to earn evil deed

347.reading: She says he knows that whatever is taught as dharma is taken up as dharma, yet does not see that teaching it earns dharma for the teacher; that flesh is a fault is no outsider's slander, and if all renounced it, who would go near killing?
347.nuance: The verse joins two points: people do what their teachers call dharma, and if all gave up flesh the killing would end. Together they make the teacher, not only the buyer, answerable for the slaughter his permission sustains.

claims.claim: if everyone renounced eating flesh, no one would kill for it
those who teach dharma gain dharma by the teaching

348.reading: She reminds him that he has even her own word, that she, standing at the head of dharma and joined to grace, drove violence away; what then does holding to cruelty gain him, and is anything more precious than the lasting life of beings? Let him think and see.
348.nuance: துரந்தனள் யான் is a woman speaking of herself, which suggests Neelakesi cites her own turning from the bloodshed of her shrine (9) as the example of a mind that gave up violence; this is a reading, not certain.

claims.claim: nothing is more precious than the life of a living being

349.reading: Finding that his defence of eating flesh can no longer stand, Mokkalan, snarling like a dog, turns to argue with the fair-browed woman against the mortification of the body.
349.nuance: காயக் கிலேசம், torment of the body, names the Jain outer austerities; the debate shifts from meat to penance because the Buddhist now attacks rather than defends. The narrator's simile of the dog shows where the poem's sympathy lies.
349.event: Worsted on eating flesh, Mokkalan angrily turns to attack the Jain practice of bodily mortification (காயக் கிலேசம்).

350.reading: Mokkalan tells her that drying in the sun, soaking in the open, giving up food in fasts and forsaking sleep night and day in a hot sea of suffering brings no gain at all, O long-eyed one.
350.nuance: The list is of the Jain outer austerities: exposure, fasting, wakefulness. The claim is answered in 354 to 358, where Neelakesi shows that the Buddhists' own ascetic practices and their praise of the bodhisattva's sufferings are hardships of the same kind.

claims.claim: hardships such as exposure, fasting and sleeplessness bring no benefit

351.reading: He argues that if some good were to be seen in wasting the body away, then burning in fire, throwing oneself from a height and wasting with disease could all be called penance, and bids her say why not.
351.nuance: A reductio: the Jain must either say what separates his fasting from self-destruction or accept the absurd conclusion. The argument assumes that pain itself is what the Jain values, which the Jain reply in 358 and 359 does not grant.

claims.claim: if wasting the body were meritorious, burning oneself, leaping from a height or wasting with disease would count as penance

352.reading: He adds that cutting one's own wounds and enduring being split, forcing open the eyes with sticks, throwing oneself from a lofty mountain, and the practices of the 'lords' who do such things, are of no use.
352.nuance: அண்ணலார் (the lords) is likely ironic, aimed at the ascetics who are honoured for such feats. The list mixes known ascetic exploits with plain self-harm to make the line between them vanish.

claims.claim: self-wounding and other extreme mortifications are of no use

353.reading: He says that if tormenting oneself were the old and good dharma, then tearing out tongues, hanging oneself to die, leaping into fire to perish and climbing the cruel red stake would all be excellent.
353.nuance: The closing image of the impaling stake (கழு) is the death of a criminal, so the argument ranks the ascetic with the condemned man. The verse ends the attack that 354 begins to answer.

claims.claim: if self-torment were dharma, self-mutilation, hanging, burning and impalement would be excellent

354.reading: Neelakesi replies by naming what his own teacher laid down: giving, conduct, forbearance, fitting vigour, flawless meditation, understanding with skill in means, the firm resolve of compassion, strength and knowledge: these are the ten perfections.
354.nuance: ஈரைம் பாரமீதை, the twice-five perfections, is the tenfold list in which skill in means, resolve, strength and knowledge follow the six of giving, conduct, forbearance, vigour, meditation and wisdom. Here the Jain debater gives the list fairly, since her point needs it to be the Buddhists' own.

claims.claim: the Buddha taught ten perfections, from giving and conduct to strength and knowledge

355.reading: She goes on with the ascetic rules his teacher gave: living at the foot of a tree, dwelling in the open, sitting and standing without lying down, wearing cast-off cloth, sleeping in the burning ground, entering houses in turn without passing any by, and eating with the rest.
355.nuance: The items match the Buddhist ascetic observances (துதாங்கம், named in 356): the debater lists them to show that Buddhism too has practices of hardship. வருச்சியார் புகுதல் seems to mean going for alms without skipping houses; the last item is unclear.

claims.claim: the monk may take up ascetic rules such as living at a tree's foot, in the open and in the burning ground, and wearing cast-off cloth

356.reading: The list ends with taking only three robes, stopping the meal at the word 'enough', sleeping on whatever place is given, not eating a second time, treating alms as a fault (?) and not going where one had planned: these, she says, are the ascetic practices the Buddha spoke.
356.nuance: துதாங்கு is the Buddhist term for these voluntary austerities and ஆத்தர் (the trustworthy one) names the Buddha as their author, so the list is presented as his own word. The fourth line is badly corrupted.

claims.claim: the Buddha prescribed the ascetic practices called dhutanga

357.reading: With the ten perfections and the ascetic practices come many hardships, she says, yet he declares that when sharp cold, sun and hunger come together, good dharma cannot join the mind.
357.nuance: She sets the Buddhists' own hard practices beside their claim that hardship keeps dharma out of the mind: the claim is answered by their own rule-book. Line 2 does not construe cleanly.

claims.claim: when cold, heat and hunger beset the body, the mind cannot hold to dharma

358.reading: She says he calls it glorious that the bodhisattva endured having slices of his flesh cut and his body split by the sword in the doing of dharma, yet with a mind that never stays on the good path he speaks against those who do great penance: a fool.
358.nuance: The bodhisattva is not named; the cutting of flesh and splitting by the sword recall the birth stories of self-giving, which the debate attacks elsewhere (214, 243, 360). Here the stories are used only to show inconsistency: the Buddhist praises bodily suffering when his own hero bears it.

claims.claim: one who praises the bodhisattva's endurance of cutting cannot consistently condemn the hardships of penance

359.reading: She says that as he holds the ten perfections to be the burden by which bodhisattvas become Buddhas, so the Jains too hold that conduct and vows are what make one a Siddha, the perfected one.
359.nuance: பாரவட்டம் and the last line are obscure. The parallel is the point: each school has a discipline that leads to its perfected state, so the Buddhist cannot call the Jain discipline mere torment without saying the same of his own.

claims.claim: the ten perfections are what bring bodhisattvas to buddhahood
conduct and vows are the means by which one becomes a Siddha

360.reading: She asks: if it is good that the bodhisattva gave himself on the great mountain to a beast hungry for flesh, though the many lives within his body die, is it good also to poison the water that many drink, saying 'may the sick man be cured'?
360.nuance: The birth story of the body given to a hungry beast is alluded to, not told (மா is any beast). The argument rests on the Jain view that a body teems with small lives, so one act of giving is many acts of killing; a Buddhist would weigh the gift by its intent, which the verse does not consider.

claims.claim: giving one's body to be eaten kills the many lives within it, and is no better than poisoning common water to cure one man

361.reading: If he answers that the giver knew the others would not die, or that poison is plainly not good, she asks how the countless lives in the giver's own body and the flesh that came to be killed are not then counted a fault.
361.nuance: The verse anticipates two replies and turns both: whatever the giver knew, the deaths in his body follow from his act. Line 1 is hard to read and the first reply is uncertain.

claims.claim: a gift of the body that destroys the lives within it is a fault

362.reading: Answering his example of hair and nails, which grow and change yet have no life, she says that hair grows only where the living soul abides in the body, and that the rising growth seen in a tree is of another kind.
362.nuance: This opens the argument on whether plants have life, a Jain tenet (trees are one-sensed beings) that the Buddhist denies. The text was repaired at line 1, and lines 3 and 4 do not construe cleanly.

claims.claim: hair and nails grow though they have no life, so growth does not prove that trees live
hair grows only while the soul dwells in the body

363.reading: You spoke of trees growing, folding up and differing in their spreading leaves, she says; these and the rest are found together in the living beings of this world as well.
363.nuance: The argument is from shared marks: what grows, closes at night and puts out leaves of different shapes behaves as the animals do. It is an inference by likeness, which the Buddhist answers with lifeless things that change (365, 366).

claims.claim: trees grow, fold and change as living beings do, and so they have life

364.reading: She takes up the 'craving' (வயா) of the growing pumpkin, a mark of life in plants, and tells him that he erred in his account of it, but the lines that give his account are obscure.
364.nuance: வயா, the craving of pregnancy, is ascribed to plants to argue that they feel. What the Buddhist said about the pumpkin and the wax and flesh of line 3 cannot be made out.

365.reading: She recalls that when it was urged that plants wilt at every touch, he answered that the hide one eats also shrinks when brought to the fire, and she asks how the change of a thing without awareness can be the same.
365.nuance: The hide example is answered again at 369, where the hide is said not to be like the living plant. சேதனை இல்லாய் may address Mokkalan as lacking sense, or describe the hide as lacking awareness.

claims.claim: lifeless things such as hide also shrink and change, so wilting does not prove that plants live

366.reading: She sets out his further reply: if trees are said to have life because their budding, flowering and power to cure grave disease show growth from their own cause, then the iron and the magnet drawing together would also be such a change.
366.nuance: The magnet is the Buddhist counter-example to the Jain argument from plants' responsiveness. Her answer to it lies beyond this chapter, so the claim is left as reported here.

claims.claim: a magnet moves iron without life, so change from a cause does not prove that plants live

links.note: Saathuvan tells the Naga chief that the faultless forbade liquor and the killing of living beings; Neelakesi argues that those who shun toddy should for the same reason shun flesh.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic's own ban joins liquor with killing, not with eating meat, and the Jain debater exploits exactly that gap, asking why the reasoning that forbids toddy stops before flesh.

links.note: Saathuvan lets the chief stop killing yet still eat beasts that die of old age; Neelakesi holds that flesh is itself a fault and that its renunciation by all would end the killing.
links.teaches: For the Buddhist story the wrong lies in the killing, so meat from a natural death is allowed, while for the Jain debater eating is wrong in itself because it is what keeps killing going; the two epics draw the line at different acts.

links.note: Kural 256 says no one would sell flesh if the world did not kill to eat; Neelakesi says that if all renounced flesh no one would go near killing, and that the teacher who teaches dharma earns its merit.
links.teaches: The couplet blames the eating world for the killing; the debate adds that a world's eating follows its teachers, so a teacher who permits flesh carries the demand argument's guilt.

gains.a: Neelakesi's bare 'if all renounced it' gains the Kural's market reasoning that links each buyer to the killing
gains.b: the couplet's faceless 'world' gains a concrete cause of its habits, the teacher whose word makes flesh-eating dharma

links.note: In 260 Neelakesi tells Arkkachandra that the eater shares the butcher's karma whatever his mind; in 344 she meets Mokkalan's same plea of innocent intention with the seller who kills for the price.
links.teaches: Against two Buddhist teachers the Jain debater answers the defence by intention in two ways, by the butcher's act and by the merchant's motive, so the epic builds a consistent case that the buyer's purpose is the cause.

links.note: The Kundalakesi fragment lists exposure, fire, cold, begging and matted hair as mere words and calls living subdued the true penance; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as profitless.
links.teaches: The Buddhist dismissal of mortification, stated in the fragment as a positive ideal of restraint, appears in the Jain epic only as a negative charge that it can then answer, so the Neelakesi keeps the attack and drops the Buddhist alternative.

links.note: Pattinattar lists the five fires, lying in water, plucking hair and going without food and says his devotees reached release without them; Mokkalan lists sun, rain, fasting and sleeplessness as bringing no gain.
links.teaches: Buddhist debater and Saiva poet reject the same austerities for opposite reasons: for Mokkalan pain has no power to free, for Pattinattar the god's name frees without it, so a shared rejection hides a disagreement about what does the freeing.

gains.a: Mokkalan's attack is seen to belong to a wider Tamil rejection of mortification, not only to anti-Jain polemic
gains.b: the poem's list of austerities, which includes plucking the hair, is seen as the Jain practice a Buddhist also attacked, so its claim of a better way enters an existing quarrel

links.note: Mokkalan says exposure, fasting and sleeplessness bring nothing; Neelakesi replies that the Buddha's own perfections and ascetic rules bring many hardships.
links.teaches: The Buddhist attack on Jain penance is met not by defending pain but by showing the Buddhist path also prescribes sleeping in the open and eating once, so the quarrel becomes one of degree rather than of principle.

links.note: In 282 Neelakesi herself says the body lives by food and awareness by the body; in 357 she mocks the Buddhist claim that cold, heat and hunger keep dharma out of the mind.
links.teaches: The Jain debater grants that the mind needs a fed body but not that it needs a comfortable one, so her two arguments mark a line between sustaining the body and sparing it.

links.note: Kural 261 makes bearing pain one half of penance; Mokkalan argues that if wasting the body were good, burning or wasting with disease would also be penance.
links.teaches: The reductio bites only if the couplet's pain is pain one inflicts on oneself; if it is the pain that comes unsought, the Kural and the Buddhist agree, so the pairing shows that the couplet's word உற்ற decides which side it is on.

gains.a: Mokkalan's argument gains a precise target: a definition of penance in which enduring pain is half the whole
gains.b: the couplet's ambiguity about whose pain is meant is shown to matter, since a rival school's objection falls on one reading and not the other

links.note: Tirumular says that even burning one's bones as firewood and frying one's flesh does not reach the Lord without melting love; Mokkalan says cutting wounds and leaping from mountains serve no purpose.
links.teaches: Both reject bodily extremity as the way, but Tirumular keeps it as a measure that love surpasses while Mokkalan declares it simply useless, so the Saiva verse still honours the ascetic's pain where the Buddhist does not.

gains.a: Mokkalan's list gains a Saiva witness that self-torment was a recognised extreme to be gone beyond
gains.b: Tirumular's hyperbole is seen against a debate in which such acts were literally practised and literally attacked

links.note: Mokkalan says that if self-torment were dharma, mutilation and impalement would be excellent; Neelakesi answers that he praises the bodhisattva for enduring having his flesh cut and his body split.
links.teaches: The Buddhist's own hero stories contain the very bodily sufferings he ridicules, so the reductio is turned on him: either the bodhisattva's endurance was folly or the Jain's is not.

links.note: In 214 Neelakesi argues that a gift of flesh or an eye cannot join another's body and so helps no one; in 360 she argues that the gift of the body to a beast kills the many lives within it.
links.teaches: The Jain case against the bodhisattva's self-giving has two prongs across the debates: the gift is useless to the receiver and murderous to the small lives in the giver, so it fails both as charity and as non-harm.

links.note: The Kundalakesi fragment calls the body a deed-made thing where swarms of worms small and grown feed and live; Neelakesi says the many lives within the bodhisattva's body die when he gives it to the beast.
links.teaches: The Buddhist verse uses the body's teeming worms to teach disgust for it, while the Jain debater uses the same teeming body to charge the Buddhist hero's gift with mass killing, so one image serves renunciation on one side and non-harm on the other.

new_concepts.gloss: a perfection: one of the virtues a bodhisattva fulfils on the way to buddhahood, counted as six or ten
new_concepts.label_source: the verses' own word: ஈரைம் பாரமீதை (354), பாரமீது (357), பாரமீதை (359)

source_issues: 343: lines 2-3 (ஈப்பவுங் கொள்பவு நேர்து மவையவை / தூப்பெனு மில்லன) do not construe with confidence.
344 line 3 (ஓவெனு முன்விலை வாணிக ரென்றினர்) is obscure; the word division may be corrupt.
346 lines 2-3 and 348 line 2 (துரந்தனள்) are hard to construe; the speaker's reference is uncertain.
356 line 4 (றுற்றியுய்த்த றன்னொடுதுதாங்கென்றாத்தர்) is run together and partly corrupt; துதாங்கு (dhutanga) and ஆத்தர் can be made out.
357 line 2 (நேருமனையி லுண்மையா னீரும்வேண்டி னீரெனக்) does not scan or construe cleanly.
362 line 1 was repaired from a TSCII leftover; lines 3-4 remain obscure.
364 is largely obscure (வயாத்திரு, மெழு கூனொடு); the opponent's argument cannot be recovered.
